eczema.name: Atopic eczema
eczema.definition: A skin condition that causes dry, itchy skin and comes and goes in flare-ups.
eczema.overview: Atopic eczema is a skin condition whose main sign is itchy, dry skin. The National Eczema Society says it affects 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults in the UK. It usually begins in early childhood. Symptoms often come and go in flare-ups, and the NHS says there is currently no cure, although symptoms tend to get better as people get older.
causes: The exact cause is not fully known.
Genetic and environmental factors, a weakened skin barrier and problems with the immune system are thought to contribute.
riskFactors: Risk is higher if a parent has the condition.
Changes in the filaggrin gene, which supports the skin barrier, are linked to it.
Pets, house-dust mites and pollen are listed among common triggers.
signs: The skin can be itchy, dry, cracked, crusty, scaly or thickened, and may blister or bleed.
Inflamed skin can look red on white skin, and darker brown, purple or grey on brown or black skin, where it can be harder to see.
Scratching can make the skin bleed and open the way to infection.
complications: Scratching can disrupt sleep.
Cracked skin can become infected with bacteria, most often Staphylococcus aureus.
Eczema can become infected with the herpes simplex virus, which can progress to a serious condition called eczema herpeticum.
People with eczema are more likely to develop hay fever, asthma and food allergy.
The NHS also lists bullying or teasing in schoolchildren and lower self-confidence among the possible effects.
eczema.diagnosis: Atopic eczema is diagnosed mainly from the skin and the history, so the diagnosis is primarily clinical. For children, NICE advises taking a history of the time of onset, pattern, severity, response to treatment, impact on the family, and personal and family history of atopic conditions. NICE says mild eczema does not usually need allergy tests.
eczema.treatment: There is currently no cure, but treatments can help manage the condition and improve symptoms. Emollients (moisturisers) are the first-line treatment during both flares and remissions, and the NHS names steroid creams or ointments for flare-ups as the other main treatment. A GP may refer the person to a dermatologist if the diagnosis is uncertain, the eczema is not controlled with current treatment or the risk of complications is high. Specialist options for moderate to severe disease include phototherapy, immune-suppressing medicines and injectable biologic medicines such as dupilumab.
eczema.prevention: Flares are managed by continuing moisturiser even when the skin improves and by identifying and avoiding triggers.
eczema.seekCare: A GP appointment is the route when symptoms appear or treatments are not helping. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised if the skin is blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or pus, painful, swollen or warm, suddenly worse or spreading, or there is a high temperature or the person feels generally unwell. If eczema herpeticum is suspected, the National Eczema Society advises seeing a doctor immediately, and using NHS 111 or A&E if a GP appointment is not possible.

sections.heading: What does atopic eczema look and feel like?
sections.body:
Itchy, dry skin is the main sign of atopic eczema. The skin can also crack, become crusty, scale, thicken, blister or bleed. Inflamed skin can look red on white skin, and darker brown, purple or grey on brown or black skin, and this can be harder to see on brown and black skin.

Symptoms often come and go in flare-ups. Severity varies widely, from small patches of dry skin to widespread inflammation with constant itching. Scratching can disrupt sleep, make the skin bleed and open the way to infection, and a cycle of itching and regular scratching may develop. The National Eczema Society says that in children the itch can be intense enough to interfere with sleep, especially at night. NICE notes that sleep disturbance is common, especially during flare-ups, and can lead to irritability and poor concentration. In babies and toddlers the eczema often shows on the face, while in older children and adults it tends to appear on the elbows, knees and hands.

sections.heading: What causes it, and what sets off flares?
sections.body:
The exact cause is not fully known. Genetic and environmental factors, a weakened skin barrier and problems with the immune system are thought to contribute. Risk is higher if a parent has the condition, and changes in the filaggrin gene, which supports the skin barrier, are linked to it. The NHS says atopic eczema is not contagious.

The NHS lists common triggers as soaps, washing detergents, some fabrics, pets, pollen, house-dust mites, heat, stress and skin infections. The British Association of Dermatologists also names dry skin, teething in babies, food allergens and airborne allergens such as pet dander, pollen, grass and house dust mites, along with stress. NICE says the role of factors such as stress, humidity and temperature extremes in causing flares is unclear, so sources do not fully agree on every trigger.

sections.heading: How is atopic eczema diagnosed?
sections.body:
Doctors mainly diagnose atopic eczema from the skin and the history, so the diagnosis is primarily clinical. For children, NICE advises taking a history of the time of onset, pattern, severity, response to treatment, impact on the family, and personal and family history of atopic conditions. Mild eczema does not usually need allergy tests, and NICE says there is no evidence that high-street allergy testing is helpful. Food allergy should be considered in children who have reacted to a food with immediate symptoms, or in infants with moderate or severe eczema that does not respond to optimum management.

NICE CKS says referral to a dermatologist should be considered if the diagnosis is uncertain, the eczema is not controlled with current treatment, or there is a high risk of complications. Children with moderate or severe eczema and suspected food allergy should be referred for specialist investigation. Psychological referral is advised when the eczema is controlled but quality of life has not improved.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
There is currently no cure, but treatments can help manage atopic eczema and improve symptoms. NICE CKS says management aims to relieve symptoms and prevent complications such as infection, and rests on skin care, anti-inflammatory treatment, and identifying and avoiding triggers. Emollients, which are moisturisers, are the first-line treatment during both flares and remissions. The NHS advises continuing moisturiser even when the skin improves, and describes emollients as products applied to the skin and also used for washing.

The NHS names steroid creams or ointments as the other main treatment, used for flare-ups. The British Association of Dermatologists says short-term use can help reduce itch during flare-ups, and that steroids and other creams are not recommended as a long-term treatment. For moderate to severe eczema, the National Eczema Society describes phototherapy as treatment with ultraviolet light, given in a hospital dermatology department once topical treatments have not controlled the eczema. Other specialist options include immune-suppressing medicines and injectable biologic medicines such as dupilumab.

sections.heading: Living with atopic eczema and the outlook
sections.body:
The National Eczema Society describes atopic eczema as a common, long-term condition that often runs in families. It usually starts in childhood and can improve as a child gets older, but it can also return at any time. The NHS says symptoms tend to get better as people get older, and that there is currently no cure.

NICE says most people with atopic eczema, more than 80%, have mild disease, and only around 2% to 4% of people with eczema have a severe form. Severity is linked to sleep, with moderate disease described as frequently disturbed sleep and severe disease as nightly loss of sleep. The NHS lists sleep problems, bullying or teasing in schoolchildren, and lower self-confidence among the possible effects, and says people with eczema are more likely to develop hay fever, asthma and food allergy. NICE CKS says that providing appropriate information is essential for managing flares and maintaining control of the condition.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help?
sections.body:
A GP appointment is the route when symptoms appear or treatments are not helping. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 if the eczema is blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or has pus-filled spots, is painful, swollen or warm, suddenly worsens or spreads, or if there is a high temperature or the person feels generally unwell.

Eczema herpeticum is a serious infection in which the cold sore virus spreads through eczema skin. NICE CKS describes rapidly worsening, painful eczema with clustered blisters and punched-out erosions. NHS Scotland guidance describes groups of little blisters that quickly break down into shallow ulcers and spread rapidly, and treats this as an emergency. The National Eczema Society advises seeing a doctor immediately if it is suspected, with NHS 111 or A&E if a GP appointment is not possible. NICE CKS says immediate hospital admission should be arranged if it is suspected.

faqs.q: Can atopic eczema be cured?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for atopic eczema, according to the NHS. Treatments can help manage it and improve symptoms, and symptoms tend to get better as people get older. The National Eczema Society says it usually starts in childhood and can improve as a child gets older, but it can also return at any time.

faqs.q: How common is atopic eczema?
faqs.a: The National Eczema Society says atopic eczema affects 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults in the UK. NICE notes that estimates vary, suggesting it may affect as many as 15% to 20% of school-age children and 2% to 10% of adults. NICE says most cases are mild. It usually begins in early childhood.

faqs.q: What is the first treatment for atopic eczema?
faqs.a: Emollients (moisturisers) are the first-line treatment, during both flares and remissions, according to NICE CKS. The NHS advises continuing moisturiser even when the skin improves, and names steroid creams or ointments as the other main treatment, used for flare-ups. A GP may refer to a dermatologist if the diagnosis is uncertain or the eczema is not controlled with current treatment.

faqs.q: Does atopic eczema affect sleep and mood?
faqs.a: It can affect sleep. The NHS notes that scratching can disrupt sleep, and NICE says sleep disturbance is common, especially during flare-ups, and can lead to irritability and poor concentration. The NHS also lists bullying or teasing in schoolchildren and lower self-confidence among the possible effects of eczema.

faqs.q: Is atopic eczema linked to asthma and hay fever?
faqs.a: The NHS says people with eczema are more likely to develop hay fever, asthma and food allergy. Mild eczema does not usually need allergy tests, according to NICE, which also says there is no evidence that high-street allergy testing is helpful. Food allergy should be considered in children who have reacted to a food with immediate symptoms.

psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
psoriasis.definition: A long-term inflammatory skin condition in which the immune system is involved, usually showing as raised red patches covered with silvery scales.
psoriasis.overview: Psoriasis is a long-lasting inflammatory skin condition that tends to come and go. The NHS says the exact cause is unknown, but a problem with the immune system, together with genes and environmental triggers, appears to play a role. Reviews link the skin patches to skin cells multiplying faster than usual. The NHS says psoriasis cannot be cured, but treatments can manage the symptoms.
causes: Skin cells (keratinocytes) multiplying faster than usual, according to medical reviews
A problem with the immune system, although the exact cause is not known
Genes and environmental triggers, which the NHS says appear to play a role
riskFactors: Stress, listed by NHS 111 Wales as a possible trigger
Drinking alcohol or smoking, also listed by NHS 111 Wales as possible triggers
Living with obesity, listed by NHS 111 Wales as a possible trigger
Certain medicines
Infections such as strep A, including a streptococcal throat infection before guttate psoriasis
Pregnancy, which NHS 111 Wales lists among possible triggers
signs: Raised red patches covered with silvery scales
Plaques that commonly appear on the scalp, knees and elbows
Nail changes such as pitting, ridging, discolouration or abnormal growth
complications: Psoriatic arthritis, a joint condition that some people with psoriasis develop
Metabolic syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease, which NICE clinical knowledge summaries say may be associated with psoriasis
Anxiety and depression
psoriasis.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually clinical, which means the GP examines the skin to check for psoriasis. An NHS source says a biopsy is sometimes needed to help find the exact cause of symptoms. NICE guidance advises referral to dermatology when the diagnosis is uncertain at first presentation, or when psoriasis cannot be controlled with topical treatment. A dermatologist is a specialist skin doctor.
psoriasis.treatment: Treatment is stepped. The NHS says mild psoriasis can be treated with creams and ointments, and that an emollient is probably the first treatment a GP will suggest. If these do not work, the NHS says light treatment (phototherapy) or stronger medicines may be needed. NICE guidance describes phototherapy with ultraviolet B light as second-line therapy. Stronger options include tablets and injections that work throughout the body, such as ciclosporin, methotrexate and acitretin, and injected biological medicines.
psoriasis.prevention: The NHS says the exact cause of psoriasis is unknown. NHS 111 Wales lists stress, drinking alcohol, smoking, obesity, certain medicines and infections as possible triggers. The British Association of Dermatologists says how these factors lead to psoriasis is not fully understood.
psoriasis.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E if psoriasis patches on the feet turn yellow-brown and fill with pus, as the NHS says this can signal a more serious condition or infection. NICE guidance says people with generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma should be referred immediately for same-day specialist assessment and treatment. NHS 111 can advise on the right urgent route when it is unclear how serious a skin change is. A GP appointment is advised for anyone who thinks they may have psoriasis, whose treatment is not working or is causing side effects, or who has joint pain, stiffness and swelling that keeps coming back.

sections.heading: What does psoriasis look like?
sections.body:
Psoriasis is described in medical reviews as a long-lasting, recurring inflammatory skin condition. Its typical appearance is raised red patches covered with silver scales. The British Association of Dermatologists lists the scalp, knees and elbows among the usual sites for these plaques, and says the scalp can be particularly itchy.

The nails can be affected too. A patient leaflet that credits the Psoriasis Association says nail involvement can include pitting, ridging of the nail surface and, at its most severe, complete nail destruction. The British Association of Dermatologists says nail psoriasis is present in about half of people with psoriasis, and that a small number of people have nail involvement only.

NHS information describes a rarer form on the feet, where pus-filled spots gradually develop into circular brown, scaly spots that peel off. The NHS says pus-filled patches on the feet that turn yellow-brown can signal a more serious condition or infection, and advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

sections.heading: What are the types of psoriasis?
sections.body:
The Psoriasis Association lists plaque, scalp, guttate, pustular, inverse and nail psoriasis among the main types of psoriasis. It also describes erythrodermic psoriasis and psoriasis in sensitive areas. NICE clinical knowledge summaries say chronic plaque psoriasis is the most common form, affecting 80 to 90 percent of people with psoriasis.

NHS inform Scotland describes guttate psoriasis as a form that sometimes occurs after a streptococcal throat infection, and says it is more common among children and teenagers. The NHS also describes a rarer form on the feet in which pus-filled spots develop.

NICE guidance says people with generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma should be referred immediately for same-day specialist assessment and treatment. It also advises referral to dermatology when nail psoriasis has a big impact on using the hands or on appearance.

sections.heading: What causes psoriasis and what sets it off?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause of psoriasis is unknown, but a problem with the immune system, together with genes and environmental triggers, appears to play a role. Medical reviews describe psoriasis as a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease, which means a type of immune cell is central to the skin changes. They link the skin patches to skin cells called keratinocytes multiplying faster than usual, with immune cells moving into the skin.

NHS 111 Wales lists stress, drinking alcohol or smoking, living with obesity, being pregnant, certain medicines and infections such as strep A among the possible triggers. The British Association of Dermatologists says the onset and severity of psoriasis have been linked to alcohol, being overweight, smoking and stress, and that these factors all appear to cause low-grade inflammation. It adds that not everyone who smokes or drinks develops psoriasis, and that how these triggers lead to the condition is not fully understood.

sections.heading: How is psoriasis diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis is usually clinical, which means the GP examines the skin to check for psoriasis. An NHS source says a biopsy is sometimes needed to help find the exact cause of symptoms. A dermatologist is a specialist skin doctor.

NICE guidance on psoriasis advises referral to dermatology when the diagnosis is uncertain at first presentation, when any type of psoriasis cannot be controlled with topical treatment, or when it has a major impact on a person's physical, psychological or social wellbeing. It says that as soon as psoriatic arthritis is suspected, the person should be referred to a rheumatologist, a specialist in joint conditions.

NHS Scotland's pathway says mild psoriasis is managed in primary care. For moderate psoriasis, it advises routine referral to a secondary care service if appropriate topical treatment has failed after four weeks.

sections.heading: How is psoriasis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment is stepped. The NHS says mild psoriasis can be treated with creams and ointments, and that an emollient is probably the first treatment a GP will suggest. Emollients are moisturising treatments that help ease itching and scaling. Sources describing NHS practice also mention vitamin D analogues such as calcipotriol and steroid creams for mild to moderate psoriasis.

If these do not work, the NHS says light treatment (phototherapy) or stronger medicines may be needed. NICE guidance describes phototherapy with ultraviolet B light as second-line therapy, and NHS sources say hospital visits are needed to receive it. Stronger medicines include tablets and injections that work throughout the whole body. The non-biological options are ciclosporin, methotrexate and acitretin, and biological medicines are given by injection.

NHS Scotland's pathway says apremilast or biological medicines are for people in whom phototherapy and first-line systemic medicines have failed.

sections.heading: Living with psoriasis and related conditions
sections.body:
The NHS says psoriasis often affects mental health, and that support from other people with psoriasis, at a local group or online, can help. If psoriasis is affecting emotional wellbeing, the NHS says a GP can arrange a referral to a mental health specialist. National charities such as Psoriasis UK offer information and support.

A Psoriasis Association article by a GP describes water and detergents such as shower gel and bubble bath as drying to the skin, and suggests lukewarm bath or shower water and plenty of emollient. Newcastle Hospitals dermatology guidance advises against putting fingers into an emollient tub, as this can introduce bacteria and cause infection.

NICE clinical knowledge summaries say psoriasis may be associated with psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, anxiety and depression. The NHS says some psoriasis treatments can harm a developing baby, so treatment may need to change for people who are planning a baby or are pregnant.

faqs.q: Can psoriasis be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says psoriasis cannot be cured, but treatments can manage the symptoms. Treatment is stepped, starting with creams and ointments for mild psoriasis and moving to light treatment or stronger medicines taken by mouth or given by injection when these do not work. A GP or dermatologist decides which approach suits an individual.

faqs.q: Is psoriasis linked to arthritis?
faqs.a: NICE says some people with psoriasis also develop a joint disease called psoriatic arthritis. The NHS describes it as causing tenderness, pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints. The NHS advises seeing a GP for joint pain, stiffness and swelling that keeps coming back, and NICE says a person with suspected psoriatic arthritis should be referred to a rheumatologist.

faqs.q: What can trigger psoriasis?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales lists stress, drinking alcohol or smoking, living with obesity, being pregnant, certain medicines and infections such as strep A as possible triggers. The British Association of Dermatologists notes that not everyone who smokes or drinks develops psoriasis, and says how these triggers lead to the condition is not fully understood.

faqs.q: When should someone with psoriasis get help?
faqs.a: The NHS advises a GP appointment for anyone who thinks they may have psoriasis, or whose treatment is not working or is causing side effects. It says to call 999 or go to A&E if patches on the feet turn yellow-brown and fill with pus. NICE guidance says generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma needs immediate referral for same-day specialist assessment.

faqs.q: Does psoriasis affect mental health?
faqs.a: NICE clinical knowledge summaries say psoriasis may be associated with anxiety and depression. The NHS says that if psoriasis is affecting emotional wellbeing, a GP can arrange a referral to a mental health specialist, and that support from other people with psoriasis, locally or online, can help.

acne.name: Acne
acne.definition: Acne is a common skin condition in which spots, from a few small ones to deep painful lumps, appear mostly on the face, chest and back.
acne.overview: Acne happens when hair follicles in the skin become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria that live on the skin can then affect the blocked follicles. Changes in hormones are a major factor, and acne tends to run in families. It can range from mild, with a few spots, to severe, with deep and painful lumps under the skin. It can also affect mental health. Treatment is available from pharmacists and GPs, and some people are referred to a skin specialist.
causes: Hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria that live on the skin can then affect the blocked follicles.
Hormone changes are a major factor.
Oil glands can be sensitive to hormones even when hormone levels are normal.
Acne also tends to run in families.
Cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage, and there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne.
riskFactors: A family history of acne.
Hormonal conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.
Some medicines, including anabolic steroids.
Skin or hair products that make the skin greasy.
signs: Blackheads and whiteheads.
Inflammatory papules and pustules.
Nodules and cysts in more severe acne.
Spots mainly on the face, chest and back.
Scarring, which can follow acne.
complications: Permanent scarring, especially if spots are squeezed or picked.
Persistent psychological distress or a mental health disorder, which NICE says can accompany acne of any severity.
Signs of skin infection in affected spots.
acne.diagnosis: The NHS grades acne by the types of spot present. Mild acne is mostly whiteheads and blackheads with a few papules and pustules, and severe acne has lots of large, painful papules, pustules, nodules or cysts, sometimes with some scarring. NICE describes acne severity as a continuum, graded as mild to moderate or moderate to severe.
acne.treatment: For a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots, a pharmacist can advise on gels or creams that can be bought without a prescription. These include products containing benzoyl peroxide. Prescription treatments include topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, azelaic acid and antibiotic tablets. The combined contraceptive pill is another option for women. NICE lists a topical treatment used together with an antibiotic tablet as an option for moderate to severe acne. Isotretinoin is a capsule treatment for severe acne that has not responded to other treatments, and the NHS says it can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor.
acne.prevention: The NHS describes gentle washing with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water as helpful for acne. NICE describes using a syndet cleansing product twice daily on acne-prone skin, choosing oil-free products and removing make-up at the end of the day. The NHS advises against squeezing spots, because this can cause permanent scarring.
acne.seekCare: A pharmacist is the usual first contact for a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots. A GP appointment is advised if self-treatment is not helping, if there are many spots, deep or painful spots, or spots that scar. A GP appointment is also advised if there are signs of skin infection, or if acne is affecting mental health. A GP can refer a person to a skin specialist (dermatologist). NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for clusters of large, hard or pus-filled lumps, or if a person starts to feel very ill. If low mood becomes serious, NHS 111 can help, and Samaritans are free on 116 123 at any time. Anyone in immediate danger should call 999.

sections.heading: What does acne look like?
sections.body:
Acne can range from mild, with a few spots, to severe, with deep and painful lumps under the skin. It usually affects the face, chest and back. The NHS lists six main types of spot: blackheads, whiteheads, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts. NICE describes acne severity as a continuum, graded as mild to moderate or moderate to severe.

Blackheads are small and black or yellow in colour. Whiteheads are similar to blackheads but do not empty when squeezed. Papules are small red bumps that may feel sore, and pustules are small red bumps filled with pus. Nodules are hard lumps beneath the skin that are sometimes painful. Cysts are the most severe type, being large lumps filled with pus, and they carry the greatest risk of permanent scarring.

The NHS grades severity by the types of spot. Mild acne is mostly whiteheads and blackheads, with a few papules and pustules. Severe acne involves lots of large, painful papules, pustules, nodules or cysts, and there may be some scarring.

sections.heading: What causes acne?
sections.body:
Acne starts when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria that live on the skin can then affect the blocked follicles. Hormone changes are a major factor, and acne also tends to run in families. The BAD leaflet says the oil glands can be sensitive to hormones even when hormone levels are normal. It also names polycystic ovary syndrome and anabolic steroids as possible triggers.

The NHS lists some medicines, such as steroids, and skin or hair products that make the skin greasy among the things that can contribute. The NHS says that cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage in the follicles. It also says there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne, and that acne cannot be passed on to other people. On diet, the BAD leaflet says a healthy, well-balanced diet is advisable, and NICE says there is little evidence to support recommending dietary changes.

sections.heading: How does skin care help with acne?
sections.body:
The NHS describes gentle washing with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water as helpful for acne. NICE advises a syndet (non-alkaline synthetic detergent) cleansing product twice daily on acne-prone skin, oil-free products, and removing make-up at the end of the day. The NHS advises against squeezing spots, because this can cause permanent scarring. NICE gives similar advice, noting that persistent picking or scratching of lesions can increase the risk of scarring.

For a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots, a pharmacist can advise on gels or creams that can be bought over the counter. The BAD leaflet lists benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid and nicotinamide as active topical treatments that are available without a prescription. It says most treatments take 2 to 4 months to have their full effect, while the NHS says many take 2 to 3 months before they start to work.

sections.heading: How is acne treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP can offer prescription treatments if pharmacy products have not worked or acne is more severe. These include topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, azelaic acid and antibiotic tablets, and for women the combined contraceptive pill. NICE lists a topical treatment used together with an antibiotic tablet as an option for moderate to severe acne. It found oral antibiotics used on their own to be less clinically effective and less cost-effective than the recommended options.

NICE recommends a structured follow-up 12 weeks after treatment starts, to monitor the response and discuss options for ongoing management. The NHS says many of these treatments can take 2 to 3 months before they start to work.

Isotretinoin is a treatment for severe acne that comes as capsules. NICE says it is considered for severe acne that has resisted adequate courses of standard treatment. Because of the risk of side effects, the NHS says isotretinoin can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor. The NHS lists dry or itchy skin among its possible side effects, and mental health problems as rare but serious ones. The NHS also says it is very important not to become pregnant while taking isotretinoin capsules and for at least one month after stopping.

sections.heading: When should someone see a doctor about acne?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if self-treatment is not helping, if there are many spots, or if spots are deep, painful or leave scars. A GP appointment is also advised if there are signs of skin infection, such as hot, swollen and red skin, or if acne is affecting mental health. A GP can refer a person to a dermatologist, a doctor who specialises in skin.

NICE lists reasons to consider referral to a dermatologist-led team, including mild to moderate acne that has not responded to two completed courses of treatment, severe acne-related scarring that persists a year after the acne has cleared, and acne of any severity that is causing or contributing to persistent psychological distress or a mental health disorder. NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for clusters of large, hard or pus-filled lumps, or if a person starts to feel very ill. In an emergency, such as someone in immediate danger, call 999.

sections.heading: What is the outlook for acne?
sections.body:
The BAD leaflet says acne usually fades by the early to mid-twenties, though it can last longer or start later in adult life. It says there is currently no cure, but effective treatment can prevent new spots and reduce scarring, and that acting early helps to avoid permanent scarring. The NHS notes that acne can take several months to improve with treatment.

The NHS says a GP can refer people to a dermatologist if acne is severe or prescription medicines are not working, or if there is scarring or a risk of scarring. NICE says referral for acne-related scarring is to a consultant dermatologist-led team with expertise in managing scarring. For severe acne, the BAD leaflet describes isotretinoin as highly effective, with about 9 in 10 people seeing significant improvement from one course, although some people relapse afterwards.

faqs.q: Is acne caused by dirt or poor hygiene?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne. It also says cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage that forms in the hair follicles. It adds that acne cannot be passed on to other people.

faqs.q: Should spots be squeezed?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against squeezing spots, because this can cause permanent scarring. NICE also says persistent picking or scratching of lesions can increase the risk of scarring. For a few spots, the NHS says a pharmacist can advise on gels or creams that can be bought over the counter.

faqs.q: Can acne be cured?
faqs.a: The BAD leaflet says there is currently no cure for acne. It adds that effective treatment can prevent new spots and reduce scarring, and that acne usually fades by the early to mid-twenties. It can last longer or start later in adult life.

faqs.q: Does diet cause or treat acne?
faqs.a: The BAD leaflet says a healthy, well-balanced diet is advisable. NICE says there is little evidence to support recommending dietary changes. The NHS describes blocked hair follicles and hormone changes as the main drivers of acne.

faqs.q: Who can prescribe isotretinoin?
faqs.a: The NHS describes isotretinoin as a capsule treatment for severe acne. Because of the risk of side effects, the NHS says it can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor. The NHS lists dry or itchy skin among its possible side effects, and mental health problems as rare but serious ones.

faqs.q: Can acne affect mental health?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says acne can affect mental health. NICE says acne of any severity can contribute to persistent psychological distress or a mental health disorder. The NHS advises seeing a GP if acne is affecting mental health. A GP can refer a person to a dermatologist.

hives.name: Hives (urticaria)
hives.definition: Hives, also called urticaria or nettle rash, is an itchy, raised rash that can appear anywhere on the body.
hives.overview: Hives is an itchy, raised rash that is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. It can appear anywhere on the body, and it may itch, sting or burn. Swelling deeper under the skin, called angio-oedema, often occurs alongside it. Hives usually gets better within a few days, although it can come back.
causes: A reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals
Other triggers can include infections, medicines, cold, heat, scratching and pressure from tight clothing
Some cases have no identifiable cause
riskFactors: Exposure to a known trigger, such as a food, a medicine or an insect sting
signs: Itchy raised bumps or patches on the skin, which can appear anywhere on the body
Swelling deeper in the skin (angio-oedema), often of the lips, eyelids or mouth
complications: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, which needs a 999 call
Difficulty breathing, which is among the emergency signs of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) that needs a 999 call
Hives that last for six weeks or more, known as chronic urticaria
hives.diagnosis: Hives is usually recognised from the appearance of the rash and the history, and routine allergy testing is not usually needed. Some blood tests may be used, mainly to rule out other conditions. For some physical types, a provocation test such as an ice cube test may be used.
hives.treatment: Mild hives often clears within a few days and can often be treated at home, and a pharmacist can advise on antihistamines. If the rash does not clear, a GP may prescribe menthol cream, antihistamines or steroid tablets, and may refer the person to a dermatologist. For longer-lasting hives, first-line treatment is a non-sedating antihistamine, and the aim is to control symptoms until the condition settles. NHS Healthier Together names chlorphenamine and cetirizine among the antihistamines it lists for children. Omalizumab is reserved for severe cases and is available in specialist clinics.
hives.prevention: Where a trigger is known, avoiding or reducing it is part of care. The BAD leaflet advises avoiding aspirin, ibuprofen and codeine unless essential, because these may aggravate urticaria.
hives.seekCare: Call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is very fast or difficult, or if there is sudden confusion or drowsiness. A GP or NHS 111 is the route if the rash has not improved after 2 days, is spreading or keeps returning, or if there is a high temperature and the person feels unwell. Otherwise a GP appointment is the route for hives that continue.

sections.heading: What are hives and what do they look like?
sections.body:
Hives, or urticaria, is an itchy, raised rash that is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. The rash can show up anywhere on the body. It may itch, sting or burn.

Some people also have angio-oedema, which is swelling deeper under the skin. The NHS describes angioedema as swelling below the skin's surface that often comes with hives. A person can have hives, angio-oedema or both. Swelling of the lips, eyelids or mouth is typical, and the BAD says it is typically painful rather than itchy. Most urticaria is not inherited. Hereditary angio-oedema is a separate condition that runs in families. Hives usually gets better within a few days.

sections.heading: What triggers hives?
sections.body:
The NHS lists many possible triggers, including certain foods, contact with plants, animals, chemicals or latex, cold, and heat from exercise, emotional stress or spicy food. Medicines, insect stings and infections can also set it off, as can scratching or pressure from tight clothing.

The BAD says the skin's mast cells release histamine, and a specific trigger is often never identified. It also says allergy is not usually the underlying mechanism, and Allergy UK says chronic spontaneous urticaria is not caused by allergy. Some cases have no identifiable cause. Chronic urticaria can be spontaneous, without a specific trigger, or inducible, in reaction to an identifiable trigger. A Leeds Teaching Hospitals leaflet lists heat, cold, pressure and emotion as possible triggers of chronic urticaria.

sections.heading: How long do hives last?
sections.body:
The BAD describes acute urticaria as an episode lasting up to six weeks. Chronic, or long-lasting, urticaria lasts for six weeks or more. Allergy UK says weals must be present daily for at least six weeks to be classed as chronic. In the NHS account, hives usually gets better within a few days.

Chronic spontaneous urticaria means that no specific trigger is found. In about half of the people with chronic spontaneous urticaria, the rash lasts for 6 to 12 months and then gradually disappears. The course in any one person is unpredictable. NICE's clinical experts described chronic spontaneous urticaria as a naturally remitting disease. A very small percentage of people with an urticarial rash have urticarial vasculitis, in which the weals last longer than 24 hours.

sections.heading: How are hives diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis is mainly clinical, based on a detailed history and the look of the rash, according to Allergy UK and a UK primary care pathway. Allergy UK says clinicians may use a symptom diary. Further tests may include evaluations of the skin, blood and urine, and testing is generally aimed at ruling out other medical conditions.

A UK primary care pathway advises against routinely referring for allergy testing, because the diagnosis is primarily clinical. The BSACI guideline says investigations depend on the clinical history and presentation, and may not be necessary. For physical types, Allergy UK says the diagnosis is usually confirmed through a provocation test such as the ice cube test. The BSACI guideline describes the ice cube test as placing an ice cube in a sealed plastic bag against the skin.

sections.heading: How are hives treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says hives can often be treated at home and that a pharmacist can advise on antihistamines. If the rash does not clear, a GP may prescribe menthol cream, antihistamines or steroid tablets, and may refer the person to a dermatologist.

For longer-lasting hives, the BAD says the aim of treatment is to control symptoms until the condition settles, rather than to cure it. Allergy UK says the first step is a daily non-sedating antihistamine. If that is not enough, it says a leukotriene receptor antagonist can be tried, and a one-off short course of steroid tablets may be offered for severe flare-ups. The BAD says omalizumab is limited to severe chronic spontaneous urticaria and is available only in specialist clinics. Allergy UK says that if initial treatment is ineffective, GPs should refer people to a specialist dermatologist or immunologist. NHS Healthier Together names chlorphenamine and cetirizine among the antihistamines it lists for children.

sections.heading: Living with hives and when to get help
sections.body:
The BAD leaflet advises avoiding aspirin, ibuprofen and codeine unless they are essential, because they may make urticaria worse.

The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is very fast or difficult, or if there is sudden confusion or drowsiness. It advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 if the rash has not improved after 2 days, is spreading or keeps returning, or if there is a high temperature and the person feels unwell. For children, NHS Healthier Together advises contacting a GP if symptoms last longer than six weeks, are hard to control even with regular antihistamines, or if there is swelling without hives. Breathing problems with hives need urgent medical help, and the route is a 999 call.

faqs.q: What causes hives?
faqs.a: The NHS says hives is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. Other triggers include infections, medicines, cold, heat, scratching and pressure from tight clothing. Some cases have no identifiable cause, according to the BAD, which says a specific trigger is often never identified.

faqs.q: How long do hives last?
faqs.a: The NHS says hives usually gets better within a few days. The BAD describes acute urticaria as lasting up to six weeks and chronic urticaria as lasting six weeks or more. In about half of people with chronic spontaneous urticaria the rash clears within 6 to 12 months, but the course in any one person is unpredictable.

faqs.q: When are hives an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is very fast or difficult, or if there is sudden confusion or drowsiness. The BAD also says breathing problems need urgent medical help, so the route is a 999 call.

faqs.q: Are hives caused by an allergy?
faqs.a: Allergy is not usually the underlying mechanism, according to the BAD, although hives can follow a reaction to things such as food, pollen or insect bites, as the NHS describes. Allergy UK says chronic spontaneous urticaria is not caused by allergy, so elimination diets are not a standard approach.

faqs.q: What is the difference between hives and angio-oedema?
faqs.a: Hives is a rash on the skin surface, while angio-oedema is swelling deeper under the skin. The NHS says angioedema often comes with hives, and the BAD says angio-oedema typically affects the eyelids, lips or mouth.

hay-fever.name: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis)
hay-fever.definition: Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, also called seasonal allergic rhinitis.
hay-fever.overview: Hay fever is a common allergy that causes sneezing, coughing and itchy eyes. It is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants. Unlike a cold, its symptoms can last for weeks or months. Asthma + Lung UK says symptoms are usually worse between March and September. The NHS says there is no cure, but symptoms can be eased.
causes: An allergic reaction to pollen from plants.
Pollen from trees, grasses and weeds is the usual trigger.
riskFactors: A family history of allergic disease is a recognised risk factor for allergic rhinitis.
Early childhood exposure to cigarette smoke has also been reported as a risk factor.
complications: Sinusitis and middle ear infection have been reported as complications of allergic rhinitis.
Allergic rhinitis is a recognised risk factor for developing asthma.
Hay fever can trigger asthma symptoms, and an NHS source says leaving it untreated raises the risk of a sudden asthma attack in people with asthma.
hay-fever.diagnosis: Hay fever is usually recognised from typical seasonal symptoms, and formal allergy testing is not usually needed. If there is doubt, a doctor may suggest blood tests or skin prick testing to confirm a pollen allergy.
hay-fever.treatment: A pharmacist can recommend antihistamine tablets, drops or nasal sprays, and steroid nasal sprays. If these do not help, a GP may refer the person for immunotherapy, which gradually builds tolerance to pollen.
hay-fever.prevention: The NHS says hay fever cannot be prevented, but symptoms can be eased. Allergy UK suggests checking pollen forecasts and showering and changing clothes after being outdoors.
hay-fever.seekCare: A pharmacist can give advice and suggest treatments for hay fever. A GP appointment is the route if symptoms get worse or do not improve with pharmacy medicines, or if they last more than two weeks and affect everyday tasks. If hay fever affects breathing or means a reliever inhaler is needed more than usual, NHS Wales advises speaking to a pharmacist, GP practice or asthma nurse. Call 999 if struggling to breathe, unable to speak in full sentences, or if a reliever inhaler is not helping.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of hay fever?
sections.body:
The NHS lists sneezing and coughing, a runny or blocked nose, itchy, red or watery eyes and loss of smell as common symptoms of hay fever. Allergy UK also lists an itchy throat or ears. MedlinePlus, a United States source, says a stuffy nose, coughing and headache can develop later.

Hay fever can look like a cold, but a cold usually clears within one to two weeks. Hay fever symptoms can last for weeks or months. Asthma + Lung UK says symptoms are usually worse between March and September, when pollen counts are highest.

Hay fever can trigger asthma symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath. NHS Wales advises speaking to a pharmacist, GP practice or asthma nurse if hay fever affects breathing or means the reliever inhaler is needed more than usual.

sections.heading: What causes hay fever, and when is it worst?
sections.body:
Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants. Allergy UK says tree pollen in spring, grass pollen in summer or weed pollen in autumn may cause symptoms, and that grass pollen is the main trigger in the UK. MedlinePlus, a United States source, names pollen from trees, weeds and grasses, and says the plants responsible vary from person to person and from area to area.

The Met Office says tree pollen comes first, from late March to mid-May. Grass pollen peaks from mid-May to July, and weed pollen lasts from June to September. It says the season starts later and is shorter in the north of the UK, where there is generally less pollen.

Allergy UK says warm, dry and windy days can lead to higher pollen counts, while rain helps wash pollen out of the air.

sections.heading: How is hay fever diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS in Devon says hay fever is usually recognised from typical seasonal symptoms. It says formal allergy testing is not usually needed unless symptoms are unusual or interfere with daily activities despite regular over-the-counter medicine, and that a symptom diary can help. One NHS-affiliated information sheet says that if there is doubt, a doctor may suggest blood tests or skin prick testing to confirm a pollen allergy.

NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP when it is unclear whether symptoms are hay fever or something else. One GP practice leaflet adds children under 2, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and symptoms in unusual patterns such as winter, when something other than pollen may be responsible.

The NHS suggests seeing a GP if symptoms are getting worse or do not improve after taking medicines from the pharmacy.

sections.heading: How is hay fever treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for hay fever and it cannot be prevented, but symptoms can be eased. A pharmacist can give advice and suggest the best treatments, such as antihistamine drops, tablets or nasal sprays, and steroid nasal sprays. The NHS describes cetirizine as a non-drowsy antihistamine used for allergy symptoms such as hay fever, and chlorphenamine as a drowsy antihistamine. Allergy UK says most people with hay fever can manage their symptoms with a daily non-sedating antihistamine.

MedlinePlus, a United States source, says nasal corticosteroid sprays are the most effective treatment for allergic rhinitis. The NHS says a GP might prescribe a steroid treatment, and may refer the person for immunotherapy if other treatments fail. Immunotherapy gives small amounts of pollen as an injection or tablet to build up immunity. It usually starts a few months before the hay fever season and may not be available everywhere.

Some local NHS areas in England, such as Frimley, say GPs no longer prescribe antihistamine tablets, steroid nasal sprays or sodium cromoglicate eye drops for hay fever. Policies vary by area.

sections.heading: Living with hay fever and getting help
sections.body:
The NHS suggests putting petroleum jelly around the nostrils, wearing wraparound sunglasses, showering after going outside and keeping windows shut when pollen counts are high. Allergy UK advises checking pollen forecasts daily and staying indoors where possible when the count is high. It also advises showering, washing hair and changing outer clothing after coming home, and not drying clothes outside when counts are high.

NHS inform and the Patient information site both say hay fever treatment works best when started early.

Allergy UK advises seeing a GP or practice nurse if symptoms persist despite antihistamines or other medicines, or if they last more than two weeks and affect everyday tasks. If hay fever affects breathing, NHS Wales advises speaking to a pharmacist, GP practice or asthma nurse. It says to call 999 if struggling to breathe, unable to speak in full sentences, or if a reliever inhaler is not helping.

faqs.q: Can hay fever be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for hay fever and it cannot be prevented, but symptoms can be eased. A pharmacist can recommend antihistamines and steroid nasal sprays. If these do not work, a GP may refer the person for immunotherapy, which gradually builds tolerance to pollen. Allergy UK says a daily non-sedating antihistamine works for most people.

faqs.q: How can hay fever be told apart from a cold?
faqs.a: Hay fever and a cold can look similar. A cold usually clears within one to two weeks, while hay fever symptoms can last for weeks or months. Hay fever commonly brings itchy or watery eyes and an itchy throat. Allergy UK advises seeing a GP or practice nurse if symptoms last more than two weeks and affect everyday tasks.

faqs.q: Can hay fever affect asthma?
faqs.a: Hay fever can trigger asthma symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath. An NHS source says leaving hay fever untreated raises the risk of a sudden asthma attack in people with asthma. NHS Wales advises speaking to a pharmacist, GP practice or asthma nurse if hay fever affects breathing, and calling 999 if struggling to breathe or a reliever inhaler is not helping.

faqs.q: When is the hay fever season?
faqs.a: Asthma + Lung UK says symptoms are usually worse between March and September. The Met Office says tree pollen comes first, from late March to mid-May, grass pollen peaks from mid-May to July, and weed pollen lasts from June to September. It says the season starts later and is shorter in the north of the UK.

faqs.q: Does hay fever run in families?
faqs.a: A family history of allergic disease is one of the strongest documented risk factors for allergic rhinitis, according to published reviews. Early childhood exposure to cigarette smoke has also been reported as a risk factor. Hay fever itself is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants.

food-allergy.name: Food allergy and anaphylaxis
food-allergy.definition: A food allergy is when the immune system overreacts to certain foods, with reactions that range from mild to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
food-allergy.overview: A food allergy happens when the immune system overreacts to certain foods. The NHS lists itchy skin or hives, swelling of the lips, face and eyes, breathing difficulties, feeling sick and tummy pain among the symptoms. A food allergy is different from a food intolerance, which does not involve the immune system. Children are most often allergic to milk, eggs, peanuts and tree nuts. Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly and needs emergency treatment.
causes: The immune system overreacts to certain foods.
Why the immune system reacts to a food is not fully understood.
The NHS lists nuts, milk, eggs, shellfish, fish, sesame seeds and kiwi fruit among common food triggers of anaphylaxis.
riskFactors: A family history of allergies, asthma or eczema raises the risk slightly.
Allergy UK says the risk can be higher when another allergic condition, such as eczema, is present.
signs: Itchy skin or hives, and swelling of the lips, face and eyes.
Feeling sick, tummy pain and diarrhoea.
Breathing difficulties, and in a severe reaction wheezing and swelling of the throat and tongue.
complications: Anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction.
Symptoms of anaphylaxis can return hours after the first reaction, known as a biphasic reaction.
food-allergy.diagnosis: The NHS lists skin-prick tests, blood tests and sometimes an elimination diet. NICE guidance for under 19s says to offer a skin prick test or blood tests for specific IgE antibodies when IgE-mediated allergy is suspected. For suspected non-IgE-mediated allergy it recommends a trial elimination of the suspected food. A GP may refer to a specialist.
food-allergy.treatment: The NHS says the main approach is avoiding the food. Antihistamines are used for mild reactions, while adrenaline auto-injectors are for severe ones, and antihistamines do not replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis. A specialist gives an allergy action plan, a written set of instructions for managing a reaction. Anaphylaxis is treated in hospital straight away, with adrenaline, oxygen and fluids given into a vein.
food-allergy.prevention: The NHS advises checking food labels carefully and telling staff at restaurants and cafes about the allergy. NHS guidance for babies says waiting beyond 6 to 12 months to introduce peanut and egg may raise the risk of allergy.
food-allergy.seekCare: Call 999 for suspected anaphylaxis, such as swelling of the throat or tongue, difficulty breathing, or feeling faint or confused, and say it is anaphylaxis. The NHS says to use an adrenaline auto-injector if one is available. For symptoms that keep coming back after eating a food, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

sections.heading: What is a food allergy?
sections.body:
A food allergy happens when the immune system overreacts to certain foods. Reactions range from mild to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Why the immune system reacts to a food is not fully understood. A food allergy is different from a food intolerance. The NHS says a food intolerance does not involve the immune system, so it cannot cause a serious allergic reaction. Intolerance symptoms, such as bloating, wind, diarrhoea and tummy pain, usually appear a few hours after eating the food.

A family history of allergies, asthma or eczema raises the risk slightly. Allergy UK says the risk can be higher when another allergic condition, such as eczema, is present.

Some people have a mix of immediate and delayed reactions to the same food. Immediate reactions are called IgE-mediated, and delayed ones are called non-IgE-mediated. Allergy UK says non-IgE-mediated reactions do not involve IgE antibodies and have a delayed onset.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a food allergy?
sections.body:
The NHS lists itchy skin or hives, swelling of the lips, face and eyes, breathing difficulties, feeling sick, tummy pain and diarrhoea. Symptoms may start straight after eating the food, or days later.

Allergy UK says symptoms of an immediate, IgE-mediated food allergy occur a few seconds or minutes after eating. Allergy UK also describes a type with both immediate symptoms, such as hives or swelling, and delayed symptoms, such as gut or skin problems. Immediate IgE-mediated reactions carry the risk of anaphylaxis.

A severe reaction is called anaphylaxis, which starts quickly and can cause breathing problems. NHS Scotland says a reaction may start mild and progress rapidly to severe. The NHS says to call 999 for signs such as sudden confusion or drowsiness, fainting, or a child who goes limp and floppy.

sections.heading: Which foods most often cause allergic reactions?
sections.body:
In children, the most common food allergies are to milk, eggs, peanuts and tree nuts. Allergy UK says food allergy in UK adults more commonly involves peanuts, tree nuts, crustaceans and plant foods. The NHS lists nuts, milk, eggs, shellfish, fish, sesame seeds and kiwi fruit among common food triggers of anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis UK says milk, egg, soy and wheat allergies that start early in life are often outgrown. Peanut and tree nut allergies are much less likely to be outgrown, and fish and shellfish allergies also tend to last.

A Food Standards Agency study, reported by Anaphylaxis UK, estimated that around 6% of UK adults, about 2.4 million people, have a clinically confirmed food allergy. In the first stage of that study, over 30% of adults reported some type of adverse reaction when eating food, but the clinical follow-up narrowed this to about 6%.

sections.heading: How is a food allergy diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS lists skin-prick tests, blood tests and sometimes an elimination diet among the ways a food allergy is investigated. A GP may refer to a specialist.

The NICE guideline on food allergy in under 19s says that when IgE-mediated allergy is suspected, a skin prick test or blood tests for specific IgE antibodies should be offered. Skin prick tests should only be done where there are facilities to manage an anaphylactic reaction. For suspected non-IgE-mediated allergy, the guideline recommends a trial elimination of the suspected food, followed by reintroduction. The NICE guideline says that serum-specific IgG testing, the vega test, applied kinesiology and hair analysis should not be used to diagnose food allergy.

NICE advises considering referral to specialist care for children who have had an acute systemic reaction or a severe delayed reaction, or who may have multiple food allergies.

sections.heading: How is a food allergy treated and managed?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main approach to food allergy is avoiding the food that causes it. Antihistamines are used for mild reactions, while adrenaline auto-injectors are for severe ones. Antihistamines do not replace adrenaline in a severe reaction. A specialist gives an allergy action plan, a written set of instructions for managing a reaction.

Day-to-day management involves checking food labels carefully and telling staff at restaurants and cafes about the allergy, according to the NHS.

For babies, NHS guidance says common allergenic foods can be introduced from about 6 months, one at a time and in very small amounts so that any reaction can be spotted. The NHS says waiting beyond 6 to 12 months may raise the risk of peanut and egg allergy. For babies with eczema or an existing food allergy, or with a family history of allergy, the NHS advises talking to a GP or health visitor first.

sections.heading: What is anaphylaxis and what happens in an emergency?
sections.body:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly. Signs can appear within minutes of contact with the trigger. They include swelling of the throat and tongue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, feeling faint or confused, and blue, grey or pale skin.

The NHS says to call 999 and say it is anaphylaxis. It also says to use an adrenaline auto-injector if one is available. The NHS describes lying down with the legs raised if feeling faint, or sitting up if breathing is difficult.

Anaphylaxis is treated in hospital straight away, with adrenaline, oxygen and fluids given into a vein. The NHS says people usually stay in hospital for around 2 to 12 hours. Before leaving hospital, people should be given 2 adrenaline auto-injectors or a prescription for them.

Symptoms of anaphylaxis can return hours after the first reaction. NHS Scotland calls this a biphasic reaction.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a food allergy and a food intolerance?
faqs.a: A food allergy involves the immune system and can cause itchy skin or hives, swelling, breathing difficulties and tummy problems. A food intolerance does not involve the immune system, so it cannot cause a serious allergic reaction. The NHS says intolerance symptoms usually appear a few hours after eating and often include bloating, wind, diarrhoea and tummy pain.

faqs.q: Can children grow out of a food allergy?
faqs.a: Anaphylaxis UK says milk, egg, soy and wheat allergies that start early in life are often outgrown. Peanut and tree nut allergies are much less likely to be outgrown, and fish and shellfish allergies also tend to last. Anaphylaxis UK publishes a factsheet called Outgrowing childhood food allergy.

faqs.q: Can a food allergy cause anaphylaxis?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says anaphylaxis can be caused by food, medicines or insect stings. It is life-threatening and happens very quickly. The NHS says to call 999 and to use an adrenaline auto-injector if one is available. Hospital treatment can include adrenaline, oxygen and fluids given into a vein.

faqs.q: How common is food allergy in the UK?
faqs.a: A Food Standards Agency study reported by Anaphylaxis UK estimated that around 6% of UK adults, about 2.4 million people, have a clinically confirmed food allergy. In the first stage of the study, over 30% of adults reported some type of adverse reaction when eating food, so more adults report reactions than have a confirmed allergy.

faqs.q: How is an elimination diet used to diagnose a food allergy?
faqs.a: For suspected non-IgE-mediated allergy, the NICE guideline recommends a trial elimination of the suspected food, followed by reintroduction. The NHS lists an elimination diet among the ways a food allergy may be investigated, alongside skin-prick tests and blood tests. A GP may refer to a specialist. NICE says serum-specific IgG testing should not be used to diagnose food allergy.

cellulitis.name: Cellulitis
cellulitis.definition: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper layers of the skin caused by bacteria.
cellulitis.overview: Cellulitis makes the skin painful, hot and swollen, and the area usually looks red, though this may be less obvious on brown or black skin. It can occur on any part of the body, but it is more common on the lower limbs. Bacteria get into the deeper layers of the skin through a break in the skin, such as an insect bite or cut. If it is not treated quickly, the infection can spread to other parts of the body, such as the blood, muscles and bones. Cellulitis is treated with antibiotics.
causes: Cellulitis is usually caused by bacteria that reach the deeper layers of the skin through a break, such as an insect bite, a cut or cracked, dry skin.
Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus are the bacteria most often involved.
Skin conditions such as eczema or athlete's foot can break the skin and make it easier for bacteria to enter.
riskFactors: Poor circulation.
A weakened immune system, for example because of chemotherapy or diabetes.
Lymphoedema, a long-term condition that causes swelling of the body's tissues.
Injecting drugs.
A wound from surgery.
Having had cellulitis before.
signs: Skin that is painful, hot, swollen and usually red.
Redness that may be less obvious on brown or black skin.
Flu-like symptoms, including feeling unwell.
complications: Spread of the infection to the blood, muscles and bones if it is not treated quickly.
Sepsis (blood poisoning), when bacteria spread from the cellulitis to the bloodstream.
Abscesses, which are collections of pus that may need draining.
Lymphoedema, because cellulitis can damage the lymphatic system.
Necrotising fasciitis, a severe and rapidly spreading infection of the muscle and connective tissue.
cellulitis.diagnosis: Cellulitis is mainly diagnosed clinically, by a clinician examining the affected area and looking for spreading red inflammation of the deeper skin. A skin swab or blood tests may be taken, although identifying the bacteria is rarely possible. Because the symptoms are similar to those of a blood clot, a doctor may ask for further tests to rule out a deep vein thrombosis.
cellulitis.treatment: Mild cellulitis affecting a small area of skin is usually treated with antibiotic tablets, usually for about a week. NICE advises oral antibiotics first when the person can take tablets and the condition does not need antibiotics given into a vein. Severe cellulitis may need hospital treatment. NHS Inform describes paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, and raising the affected area when sitting or lying down.
cellulitis.prevention: People at higher risk can help prevent cellulitis by treating skin problems such as eczema and athlete's foot, and by keeping weight at a healthy level. NICE advises against routine antibiotics to prevent cellulitis coming back, although people who keep getting it may be prescribed long-term antibiotics.
cellulitis.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for signs of serious complications, such as a very high temperature, a fast heartbeat or breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, or loss of consciousness. For skin that is painful, hot and swollen, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111. Cellulitis in the eye is very serious, so urgent assessment through NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment is the usual route, with 999 or A&E for the emergency signs above. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly at any time, or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of cellulitis?
sections.body:
Cellulitis makes the skin painful, hot and swollen. The area usually looks red, but this may be less obvious on brown or black skin. It can occur on any part of the body, but it is more common on the lower limbs, and less commonly affects the arms or torso. Some people also feel unwell with flu-like symptoms, and may have swollen, painful glands. The skin may blister.

NHS 111 Wales also describes red streaks spreading from the affected area. Symptoms may get worse in the first 48 hours of treatment before they start to improve. Changes in skin colour can persist after cellulitis, and are more common if it has affected the same area more than once. Cellulitis is not passed from person to person, because it affects the deeper layers of the skin.

Cellulitis in the eye is very serious. The route to care for cellulitis near the eye is described in the last section of this article.

sections.heading: What causes cellulitis and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Cellulitis is an infection caused by bacteria getting into the deeper layers of the skin. A break in the skin, such as an insect bite, a cut or cracked, dry skin, lets the bacteria into the deeper tissues. The bacteria most often involved are streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus.

The NHS lists poor circulation, a weakened immune system, lymphoedema, injecting drugs, a wound from surgery and having had cellulitis before as risk factors. A weakened immune system can be due to chemotherapy or diabetes. NHS Inform adds that being overweight can increase the chance of developing cellulitis or slow recovery from it. Skin conditions such as eczema, or a fungal infection of the feet called athlete's foot, can break the skin and make it easier for bacteria to enter. The British Association of Dermatologists lists lymphoedema both as a risk factor and as a complication. Once someone has had cellulitis, it is more likely to return in the same part of the body.

sections.heading: How is cellulitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
Cellulitis is mainly diagnosed clinically, by a clinician looking at the affected area. Diagnosis is usually made from the clinical picture, based on spreading red inflammation of the deeper skin. A skin swab or blood tests may be taken, although identifying the bacteria is rarely possible. NICE notes that in most cases swabbing of cellulitis gives negative results, especially when the skin is intact.

A UK hospital leaflet says that because the symptoms are similar to those of a blood clot, a doctor may ask for further tests to rule out a deep vein thrombosis. Other skin conditions, such as venous stasis dermatitis and contact dermatitis, can look like cellulitis. Erysipelas is a related infection that affects the upper layers of the skin, while cellulitis reaches deeper tissue. The two can overlap, so a definite diagnosis is not always possible. Cellulitis tends to have ill-defined borders and develop more slowly, while erysipelas has better-defined borders and develops faster.

sections.heading: How is cellulitis treated?
sections.body:
Mild cellulitis affecting a small area of skin is usually treated with antibiotic tablets, usually for about a week. NICE advises oral antibiotics first when the person can take tablets and the condition is not severe enough to need antibiotics given into a vein. If antibiotics are given into a vein, NICE advises a review by 48 hours and a switch to tablets if possible. For infection near the eyes or nose, NICE suggests a different first-choice antibiotic and says specialist advice may be sought.

If cellulitis is severe, the person might need hospital treatment with antibiotics given into a vein. NHS Inform describes paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, and raising the affected area on a chair or pillow when sitting or lying down. NHS Inform also says that stopping antibiotics early can cause cellulitis to come back. Symptoms may get worse in the first 48 hours of treatment before they begin to improve. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly at any time, or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days.

sections.heading: Can cellulitis cause complications or come back?
sections.body:
Most people make a full recovery with no long-lasting effects. If cellulitis is not treated quickly, the infection can spread to other parts of the body, such as the blood, muscles and bones. Infection that spreads to the blood can cause blood poisoning, also called septicaemia or sepsis. In severe cases an abscess, a collection of pus, can form and may need draining. Necrotising fasciitis is a severe and rapidly spreading infection of the muscle and connective tissue. Cellulitis can also damage the lymphatic system, which can cause permanent swelling of the affected arm or leg.

Cellulitis can come back. The British Association of Dermatologists notes that it is more likely to return in the same part of the body, and that fixing skin breaks such as athlete's foot or eczema can help. NICE advises that antibiotics should not be offered routinely to prevent it coming back. NHS Inform says people who keep getting cellulitis may be prescribed long-term antibiotics, and may be referred to a dermatologist, a skin specialist.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help for cellulitis?
sections.body:
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for skin that is painful, hot and swollen. NHS 111 Wales lists rapidly spreading redness among the signs for which urgent help through NHS 111 is advised.

The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for signs of serious complications. It lists a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, a fast heartbeat or breathing, purple patches on the skin, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, and loss of consciousness. It advises against driving to A&E in this situation; someone else can drive, or 999 can be called for an ambulance.

Cellulitis in the eye is very serious. Cellulitis near the eyes or nose can need specialist advice, and urgent assessment through NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment is the usual route, with 999 or A&E for the emergency signs above. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly at any time, or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days of starting antibiotics.

faqs.q: How long does cellulitis take to get better?
faqs.a: NHS Inform says most people make a full recovery after 7 to 10 days. Mild cases are usually treated with antibiotic tablets for about a week. Symptoms may get worse in the first 48 hours of treatment before they start to improve. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days, or worsen rapidly or significantly at any time.

faqs.q: What is the difference between cellulitis and erysipelas?
faqs.a: Erysipelas affects the upper layers of the skin, while cellulitis affects the deeper layers. Cellulitis tends to have ill-defined borders and develop more slowly, while erysipelas has better-defined borders and develops faster. The two can overlap, so a definite diagnosis is not always possible, and NICE guideline NG141 covers both.

faqs.q: Can cellulitis be mistaken for a blood clot?
faqs.a: A UK hospital leaflet says the symptoms of cellulitis are similar to those of a blood clot. For that reason a doctor may ask for further tests to rule out a deep vein thrombosis. Other skin problems, such as venous stasis dermatitis and contact dermatitis, can also resemble cellulitis.

faqs.q: Can cellulitis come back?
faqs.a: Cellulitis can come back. The British Association of Dermatologists notes it is more likely to return in the same part of the body, and that fixing skin breaks such as athlete's foot or eczema can help. NICE advises against offering antibiotics routinely to prevent it. NHS Inform says people who keep getting cellulitis may be prescribed long-term antibiotics.

faqs.q: When does cellulitis need emergency care?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for signs of serious complications. These include a very high temperature, a fast heartbeat or breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, and loss of consciousness. Cellulitis in the eye is very serious. Painful, hot and swollen skin that is not an emergency still needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

conjunctivitis.name: Conjunctivitis
conjunctivitis.definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the clear tissue that covers the white of the eye and lines the inside of the eyelids.
conjunctivitis.overview: Conjunctivitis, often called pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the clear tissue over the white of the eye and inside the eyelids. It leaves the eye red, and the eye may feel gritty, sticky or watery. NHS inform names three common causes: infection, an allergic reaction and irritation. The NHS says it usually gets better within a couple of weeks without treatment. A NICE briefing says antibiotics are not needed for most people with infective conjunctivitis.
causes: Infection with a virus (viral conjunctivitis), which NICE describes as the most common cause of infective conjunctivitis
Infection with bacteria (bacterial conjunctivitis)
An allergic reaction to allergens such as pollen, dust mites or pet dander (allergic conjunctivitis)
Irritants such as chlorine or make-up, or something in the eye such as a loose eyelash (irritant conjunctivitis)
Some sexually transmitted infections, which the NHS says can cause conjunctivitis that takes longer to get better
riskFactors: Close contact with someone who has infectious conjunctivitis, because it can spread easily from person to person, for example on shared towels
signs: A watery red eye in viral conjunctivitis
A red eye with a sticky yellow discharge in bacterial conjunctivitis
Pus that sticks to the eyelashes in infective conjunctivitis
Swollen eyelids in allergic conjunctivitis
complications: Viral conjunctivitis occasionally causes inflammation of the cornea or scarring of the conjunctiva, which can affect sight, though Moorfields says this usually responds well to treatment
Adenoviral conjunctivitis usually clears on its own, but NICE says a person can stay infectious for up to 14 to 21 days after infection
Repeated infection with trachoma, a chlamydial eye infection that begins as conjunctivitis, can scar the conjunctiva and lead to vision loss
conjunctivitis.diagnosis: Viral conjunctivitis tends to cause a watery red eye, while bacterial conjunctivitis is more likely to cause a sticky yellow discharge, according to Moorfields. NICE says further tests such as a swab may be needed if the condition persists, does not respond to treatment or to help decide on treatment. NICE has also published a briefing on a point-of-care test for diagnosing adenoviral conjunctivitis.
conjunctivitis.treatment: Most cases get better on their own. Home care described by the sources includes cleaning the eyelids with clean water or a warm flannel, using a cold compress and avoiding contact lenses until symptoms have cleared. Antibiotics do not work against a virus or an allergy, and antihistamines can ease allergic symptoms. A pharmacist can advise on eye drops or antihistamines.
conjunctivitis.prevention: The NHS advises avoiding rubbing the eyes, washing the hands often and not sharing towels or pillows. UKHSA gives the same hygiene advice and also names flannels.
conjunctivitis.seekCare: The NHS says eye pain, sensitivity to light, changes in vision such as wavy lines or flashing, or very red eyes call for an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111, as these can be signs of a more serious eye problem. Moorfields advises contacting Moorfields Direct or going to a local A&E if vision becomes more blurred, eye pain becomes noticeable or blisters or spots appear on the eyelids. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment for a baby under 30 days old with red, sticky eyes. A GP appointment is advised if symptoms have not cleared within 7 days.
